translations.text: May pleasant blessings come to Salomo the good, who is now bishop of the noble see of Constance;
may he who called him to that office double upon his head all the good that the bishops who were there before him had!
I send you a reading of this book into the kingdom of the Swabians, so that you may examine it thoroughly and decide whether it ought to be of use;
if you find anything here that is worth reading, may your mind, full of wisdom, ponder it.
Your learning, your wisdom, was often very useful to me in the past; for that I give great praise.
I often call to mind the many good things that you taught me earnestly with your own words.
Not that my abilities could ever have earned it, or have won such favor in those matters;
it was done by your noble kindness, your own goodness, your provision, and not at all by my deeds.
Now above all I shall continually ask the Lord to repay you for it with a reward, and with his own word;
may he give you the rest of Paradise to delight you. He who held fast to God's law has never gone unrewarded.
In the beauty of the kingdom of heaven may it be your reward, with an abundance of recompense, that you gave me instruction.
If there is anything in this book that any man might care for, of words or of good things, anything that pleases your mind:
in your mind, turn that to your own credit on account of your instruction, and count it, without wavering, wholly to your merit.
It often happens that when a man's disciple does good, the good teacher profits greatly by it.
May Peter the mighty reward you gladly for it, he for whom the Lord dug a grave at Rome and gave house and court;
may Christ the good himself always send you pleasant blessings in joy from heaven above!
If I dare to make so bold, I shall not leave it at all of that, but shall always gladly ask his grace for you,
that he may raise up your dignity with his own favor and fix his manifold goodness firmly in your heart;
may he grant you his kingdom, the high kingdom of heaven, because the good man here always wept and continually called upon God;
may he guide you both there early, and join me to it, so that we may rejoice there in God's eternal year,
may he gladden us in heaven so that we escape punishment; and may he show us that kindness through his goodness!
May he do it for our good, with a glad heart! Born in good fortune was he who ever found that blessedness there,
for he will never again fail (believe me in this) to rejoice in his heart there forever in good things.
May Christ the good himself kindly grant us here that we may ever be glad at heart in the eternal good!
HERE BEGINS THE FIRST BOOK OF THE GOSPELS, WRITTEN IN GERMAN BY THE GRACE OF THE LORD. Here begin the chapters.
For us the days of bearing children are long past; heavy old age makes it hopeless for us.
Much of our youth has passed over us; old age does not give us what youth should have given.
How then can I know that a child will come to us? For in old age it has been taken from us, right up to the end."
Then the messenger of God spoke, though not in anger; he told him the same message again:
"I am one of the seven, of God's beloved messengers, who stand always in his sight,
whom he sends here into the world when he works mighty deeds, and they make known very weighty works.
He sent me from heaven to tell you this very thing, from the height of the heavenly kingdom, so that I might make it known to you.
Now, since you scorn the message so strongly, you shall at once become mute, until you see it truly come to pass;
because you are contrary to God's message, and you also deny what God himself is giving.
It will be fulfilled nonetheless, at the time God has set; until then you will sorely lack your words."
The people were standing outside, and they wondered greatly why the priest was taking so long;
why he did not tell them that God had accepted the prayer, and did not bless them with his hand.
Then he came out late, badly frightened; he had been struck dumb, because he did not believe.
Then he made signs, without speaking, that the crowd of people should go home.
They left in sorrow and also pondering, because he told them nothing of the wonder he had seen there.
When the days of the offering came to an end, he too went straight away to his home.
Grieving for his speech, he rejoiced in the hope; he believed very late, and so he had to wait so painfully.
The woman was carrying a son and was very ashamed that in her old age she would have to go about with a child in hand.
5. THE ANGEL GABRIEL WAS SENT.
After this there passed, as it might be, half a year: by count of months, three times two.
Then came a messenger from God, an angel from heaven; he brought this world a precious message.
He flew the sun's path, the road of the stars, the ways of the clouds, to the holy lady;
to the noble lady, Saint Mary herself, whose forebears had all been kings, generation after generation.
He went into the palace and found her sorrowful, with the psalter in her hand, which she was singing through to the end;
she was weaving fine cloths from precious yarn, which she always did gladly.
Then she gladly offered her maidenly breasts; she did not hold back but showed them, and she suckled the Son of God.
Blessed were the breasts that Christ ever kissed, and the mother who spoke to him and constantly kept him covered;
Blessed was she who nursed [?] him and set him in her lap, who gently lulled him to sleep and laid him beside her!
Blessed was she who clothed him and cared for him, and who lies in bed with such a child;
Blessed was she who protected him when the frost hurt him, her arms and hands embracing him!
There is no one on earth who could sing her praise to the end, nor any man ever so zealous that he could recount all her goodness;
There is no one the day touches or the sun shines on who could ever finish it, even if he began it!
For her good son graciously glorifies her; her praise and renown are such that you cannot count them.
She is a glorious mother, and yet truly a virgin; she bore for us the most perfect heavenly Lord.
Mystically. The Lord chose to come at the time when the whole world was being counted, so that all of us alike would be enrolled in the kingdom of heaven.
They laid him in a manger, where the cattle were fed, because he wishes to provide for us and lead us to the eternal feast.
If that birth had not happened, the world would have been lost; Satan would have taken it if he had not come then.
We were in bonds, in hostile hands; you, Lord, gave us help in our utmost need!
XII. And there were shepherds in the same region.
There were shepherds in that land, keeping watch over the livestock to guard them against enemies.
A beautiful messenger came to them, a shining angel, and they were lit up by heavenly light.
They were suddenly afraid when they saw him, and the words of God's messenger startled them greatly.
God's messenger spoke at once: "I am going to tell you something wonderful: salvation will come to you from God, and you have nothing to fear.
I am going to give you a message that the God of heaven commanded, and no one has ever heard so lordly a message.
Because of it his world will be joyful forever, and so will all creation in the world that walks on this earth.
This land has had the heavenly Savior newly born to it, that is the good Lord Christ, from a young mother,
In Bethlehem. The kings all came from there, and from them his mother was born too, the fair maiden.
Good men, I will tell you how you will find him, and a sign is fitting too, because of the wonder of it.
Go from here to the town. As I told you, you will find a newborn child lying in a manger."
Then, while he was speaking to them, a host of angels came, a heavenly multitude, all singing like this:
In the height of the kingdom of heaven, glory be to God, and on earth peace also to all who are full of good will!
Mystically. They announced the good news to us early, and also taught a song with it. Consider within your heart what this verse sings:
Do not let the desire for evil will into your breast, so that it does not take away from you the peace in the kingdom of heaven.
We should practise that song; it is a beautiful way of receiving God, because the angels brought it to us from heaven as an example.
A bishop who keeps watch over Christian people is also worthy of the beautiful sight of angels.
The angels flew back to heaven, singing, into the sight of the Lord; that was fitting for them.
XIII. THE SHEPHERDS SPOKE TO ONE ANOTHER.
Then the shepherds, those same keepers of the herds, spoke (they were considering the message, those same words of the angel):
"Let us all hurry now to the town, so that we too, with the country people [?], may see that word of God
that the Lord wished to bring about and sent here into the world; indeed, the gracious God showed us the message first."
Then they went quickly and in great haste; they set out very early, and their minds were firmly set on it.
When they came there, they saw the mother; she had set the best of children in her lap;
and also the man who had brought her there, who watched over the two of them; it had to be so, that he served them.
They saw the word there and recognized it at once, which the angels had shown them where they were tending the cattle.
All who heard it were greatly amazed, and they also felt more fear when the shepherds told this.
The mother kept the words firmly in her breast, pondering this carefully in her heart and mind:
how the words that the prophets had spoken before were coming to pass here, and how all this had also come about so fittingly.
Then the shepherds went straight back home on their way; they rejoiced greatly at the true words.
They had found it all there just as the angels had told them; for this each of them praised the Lord gloriously.
XIV. ON THE CIRCUMCISION OF THE CHILD AND ON THE PURIFICATION OF SAINT MARY.
When the eighth day came during which she had nursed the child, they had to fulfil the law willingly,
the custom that the old forefathers had always kept. They also knew how things stood with the name; they called him Savior,
as the angel had told them and shown it to them before she was with child.
The name is well meant, because he heals the people. The angel had announced it before, and the meaning of the name is explained there.
The law commanded the people very strictly (and we too should now fulfil it willingly and constantly),
"Also do with it what the law teaches you, so that nothing the prophet wrote is left undone;
By this you act toward God so that he is merciful to you; and if you begin it, you will win his favor!"
We must heed these words, strive hard toward them as well, and fulfill them with great willingness.
What he teaches them here is now directed to us; we cannot turn aside from it, we must take it to heart!
Whoever among men repents and regrets his sins, and then truly does so, heaps up much good for himself;
And if he then faithfully fulfills what God above commanded here, he is (I tell you openly) the Lord's own beloved.
XXV. Jesus comes from Galilee to John.
Christ came from his homeland to the gathering, so that John might meet him there and wash him with baptism.
Then the dear prophet quickly drew back; he spoke out plainly and strongly resisted it.
"Lord," he said, "how can it be (for I am your lowly servant!) that my hands should touch you to baptize you?
It is rather you who should touch me and baptize your servant; how can I presume, then, that this office should be mine over you?"
Then the Son of God himself spoke gently to him and told him that he wished it, and that it had to be so.
"Let it be done this way, as we have now said; it is fitting for us to fulfill willingly everything that is good."
He quickly carried it out, as the Lord Christ wished; then he baptized him, as was required and as he himself had commanded him.
Then heaven was opened; he heard the Father speak, and there he gladly told of the goodness of that same Son.
"This is my dear Son, and in my heart dearer still; in him I am fully pleased, that I begot him such.
Adam once rejected me and also brought himself to ruin; I believe that this one fulfills everything I will.
He behaved as he should not have, and did what I did not wish; but this one wills everything, as my only Son should."
He saw the Spirit of God coming from the kingdom of heaven, as you know; it settled upon Christ as soon as he had washed him.
It was like a dove; that was most fitting, because of the dove's goodness and gentleness.
There is no gall in it at all, and nothing bitter; it does not fight with its beak, nor does it claw with its feet.
So is the Holy Spirit: in him is all beauty in the highest degree, sweetness and goodness and kindly gentleness.
XXVI. Moral interpretation (Moraliter).
Baptism benefits us all; the water is consecrated, since the Lord Christ came home to us and purified it with his body.
Since he bathed in it, he purified the spring; since then, salvation has awakened in the waves for all people.
He readily gave them an answer in return; he did this to each one very boldly.
"I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: make straight his path for God, as the prophet said!"
They did not understand the teaching, and so they asked further; they did not tire of words, and they were sorely troubled [?] by it.
"Why do you go about and baptize, since you are not the Savior, nor yet one of those men whose office this is?"
He answered each of them manfully and at once made it plain to them that it was his office.
"Whoever among men wishes it, I gladly baptize him, and I consecrate each one; I do not refuse anyone the waters.
Yet you have no need on that account [?]; the man is now among you whose words declare what these works signify.
You know nothing of him; but this is my errand, that I should tell you what he intends here.
He comes after me, and yet he was before me for all time; whoever is foremost in the land, he is that one's lord.
So high is his majesty that I do not think I could be worthy to touch his shoe-straps to untie them;
or to kneel humbly before his feet so that I might loosen the straps that bind them.
He will baptize you, though you do not know it, through the Holy Spirit, and will soon cleanse you in shining fire.
He holds his winnowing fan in his hands so that he may cleanse his grain very thoroughly;
sweep his threshing floor and cast away the chaff, so that the grain shines and no refuse [?] touches it;
so that he may gather it all into his barns and then burn the chaff in fire."
I know that once the messengers had done their errand, they decided to set out and go home.
XXVIII. SPIRITUALLY.
With all our strength let us now pray to the Lord that he will not, to our sorrow, separate us from the good;
that we may not be parted in sorrow from the joyful, and may never have to see ourselves among those in grief;
that the winnowing fan may be a help to us at the Judgment and not blow us away forcibly forever;
and that afterward we may never burn there in fire like chaff, but by his grace escape that woe;
that his shepherds may watch over us and always keep us, and not winnow us out from among God's grain;
so that we, rich in good works, may be gathered with God's beloved servants into the high kingdom of heaven,
into high glory, which is the kingdom of heaven; and may escape this misery for the sake of eternal bliss,
and with the beloved may enjoy the kingdom of heaven, and enjoy in blessedness that ever-sweet granary,
"I declare to you," he said, "(as you have heard me say before, and I say it no less now) that I myself am not Christ.
I am his own messenger. My mission also goes before him, so that I, out of nothing [?], may direct the people onto the way.
Truly, he who has the bride is the bridegroom, and he keeps his love for his beloved.
His friend, who stands there at once [?], listens to his word and hears the bridegroom's voice with love.
He disregards nothing of what the bridegroom says to him, and always rejoices gladly at that voice.
That is my blessed state of mind and my joy, so good: in him all my joys are made full for me!
He shall grow greatly by his own deeds, so that my works dwindle before his powers.
He who is from the earth here shall speak from where he is; he will surely talk of earthly things.
But he who does not come from there, and came from heaven above, has power that extends mightily over all the lands of the world!
My preaching is nothing but what I have been commanded to preach. But what he teaches, he sees and hears it all himself.
Yet people will not accept that kindness [?] or practise it in their hearts, so as to believe in him.
Those who do come to it receive faith in him, and they make it widely known that he was always the Lord.
The Father loves his Son. He himself sent him here and gave everything into his hand, into his power.
He does not measure out his goodness to him as he does to us sinners. He shares it with him and imparts his Spirit to him,
because he is his own child. Whatever is dearest to him (I tell you this for certain), he gives him all of it entirely.
The man who learns this and turns his faith toward him makes his mind very glad for all eternity.
But whoever does not do this will come to a sorrowful mind, and God's wrath remains upon him!"
Truly, John was not yet lying in prison when this was preached in this way, all spoken by him like this.
XIV. JESUS, WEARY FROM THE JOURNEY.
After these things Christ went to his home country, into his own region; the books tell us this.
He grew weary from the journey, as often happens to someone travelling. Hardships give no respite to anyone who is truly a man.
He travelled through Samaria and came there to a town, and in his haste he came to a resting place.
Then he sat down weary, as we told here earlier, by a well (which we also call a "puzzi").
The evangelist says there that it may have been the sixth hour, which is the hottest part of the day and the time of greatest hardship.
His disciples hurried off and fetched food by buying it, so that they could set about eating with Christ himself. Until [?]
Christ taught this truly, and much more besides; I tell you in truth: you can read it yourself there,
all his admonitions and his very full teaching, and also very heavy threats; this I tell you in truth.
No one can recount it all, even if we begin it; the goodness of that teaching was very pleasing.
When he had then come to that point, he went down from the mountain; the whole multitude of the people followed him plainly.
He himself then intended, when he healed a leper at once with his words, where all the people saw it,
that they might take great delight in it, and that the teaching which they had heard in there meanwhile might be firm in them;
that they might wake early and think hard about it, and that it might be firm within their breasts;
that their minds might not waver, that they might be firm in their thoughts, in mind and in spirit, for every good.
Lord, make it useful to us, so that it may sit well with us; shield us from harm, do not separate us from your own;
so that we may not fall away from all your beloved ones, from your own dear friends; may we avoid that peril!
Purify our thoughts (we are your servants) with abundance of grace from the sickness of sins;
Hold us safe in our need from all adversities, so that we may shun perverse thoughts!
Shield us swiftly from all misdeeds, from terrible sicknesses, with your own power!
Your words here above, which tell us the whole account: for these grant us a very good mind and spirit;
grant us all, Lord, that we may always want what is yours, and always fulfil with deeds what your words tell us;
that we may think on it and lay it in our hearts, and leave out nothing of it, but make it cleave there!
Drive all misdeeds swiftly from us; fasten this in our minds, so that it may turn out for our good,
so that we may work at it with watchful thoughts, and always heed it with pure thoughts!
May harm flee quickly, and may this always draw near to us, and may we bring about by it that you may thank us for it;
that we may be joined, every one of us, to your own, who did you service here as they prayed to you, Lord;
and that we may be glad in the eternal life with your servants forever (we desire nothing more),
with your angels; that we may escape woe, in the kingdom of heaven, rightly, in your sight;
from age to age with the blessed souls, from world to world, may we be praising you forever! Amen. Here ends the second book.
I. Preface of the third book.
II. There was a certain royal official.
I. Preface to the Third Book.
With Christ's own blessings I now wish to tell here, in a little book, especially of the wondrous miracles
(of the Wondrous One) which he performed here in the kingdom, while he was here in the world, before he tasted death for our sake;
the wondrous signs, some of them at least, truly, for even if he wished to, there is no man who could recount them all.
I do not write now strictly in the order in which they occur there, but as the deeds come into my mind.
With fearful cares I pray for his grace, that he may also work his sign in this work,
so that in these books I never go astray, and that I write the Lord's deeds here rightly and beautifully.
He made the lame run and the dumb men cry out too: may he see to it that I do not limp here, and do not waver in the meaning either.
Healer of lepers: may he also cleanse me here of pus and of wounds, of my grievous sins!
In them, alas, I remember much sorrow and pain; my heart weeps, their pain does this to me.
Lord, I must badly escape from the stench: take me (do not do it too late!), as you did Lazarus!
You brought him back to life from death, you awakened the body: bring to life in me (that is more) my weary soul,
so that I may come to understanding here in this life, and also sit at your table, as he did afterwards: may I hope for that;
that I may always be attentive and careful in the books, and in them also think fully of your own will!
And what I now tell here is entirely your gift; increase my understanding for your own honour.
Do not avenge my sin in this, Lord, but grant me understanding for it; nothing here gladdens our heart as your forgiveness does!
Gently, my dear Lord, let the chastisement be; soothe my heart, as a mother does to her little child.
Though she may beat it sorely, she never wishes (rather, she protects it) that anyone else should wound it.
She at once puts her hand in front of it if anyone aims at it there; she is at once mindful of the way of her dear child.
With her hand she shields it, the same hand with which she beats it; her heart cannot bear to see what an enemy does to it.
The father too does the same: though he grieves its heart sorely, he still keeps its noble inheritance for its benefit.
Protect me likewise, Lord, so that I may surely be your servant; may your hand also defend me, so that the enemy may not harm me!
Grant me also hope of my homecoming; be father and mother to me, you are my good Lord!
II. There was a certain royal official.
When Christ came into Galilee, the news spread, as was fitting, and his power was made known throughout all that land.
The exalted servants of God gather up the words for them; they fix in writing what people like me leave behind.
Wherever it happens that someone like me does not understand it, they collect it into books, to be kept and held there,
so that it may be read there, preserved, year after year: what they finely told us and laid in the baskets.
By this they have shown why they are called baskets: because their goodness endures poverty here.
A basket is a servant's vessel; yet they do not mind it if people ever call them baskets in this way,
for they are all full of Christ's teaching, that same subtle wisdom which they write down for our benefit.
The grass is the vices, the lusts of the body; they bloom here in a person, soon to wither.
We must set about always subduing such grass and treading all its sweetness under foot,
so that by this deed it withers away completely beneath us and does not rise up again against us, contrary to what is right.
We cannot sit down at Christ's feast, even if we want to and even if we make a start, unless we ourselves understand [this].
As I said, tread all that sweetness under your feet, so that it does you no harm at all and does not hinder you at the feast.
When you have done that, Christ's food will grow for you in mouth and in mind, for your own good.
Read gladly in the hardness of the letters, and dig carefully into the plainness of the scripture:
there you will always, without fail, find very spiritual bread under the crust, so that you will take great delight in it.
If you do this very often, Christ's food will grow for you continually; that is how it does a person good.
If you keep sitting longer up there at those words, then perverse thoughts will wither away in you more and more, without fail,
and the grass under you will rise up against you less; the evil lusts will give you respite from then on.
And there you will also, without doubt, find a very precious treasure: the famous prophet who made the bread multiply.
The people proclaimed that he was a prophet; but faith has come to us that he is himself the Son of God.
May he deign to gladden us always at his feasts, keep us from hunger and also save us from death!
VIII. THE PEOPLE WANTED TO MAKE HIM KING, AND HOW HE WALKED ON THE SEA.
Then the people wanted to seize him by force (truly, I will not hide it from you) and make him king over them.
He fled into the mountains to hide himself there. He certainly did this because his time had not yet come
for him to be king with power, openly and in truth; that is why he fled from them there.
He then commanded the disciples to go to the other side, to stay watchful, and to cross over the sea.
These princes and the highest men will do it: they will hand me over by force to a foreign people.
After that I will rise (do not be afraid of it; truly, it will not be long) at once on the third day."
When Peter heard this, he took him aside and rebuked him, and very harshly too, with words like these:
"Lord, do not speak of it any further; have mercy on yourself, so that the world never sees such a thing happen to you!
Lord, you should not want to fall in this way; and you yourself should forbid the people to do this to you.
Do not betray us like this by ever failing us; God forbid that such a thing should ever happen to you!"
Then he gave an answer that seemed harsh to Peter, and it certainly stung him very sharply.
"Get behind me, then, you satan of a man! You know nothing of the counsel that the Lord himself wills most.
He has resolved that the world be healed through me. It cannot happen any other way, and you say you do not want it!
Human deeds matter more to you than his counsel. You go by what seems right to you, not by what he intends.
Whoever wishes to follow me gladly at all times must utterly deny his own self-will,
and take up his cross as well, and then always follow me wherever I go before him.
What does it help a wretched man who rules so widely here that all the ends of the world are in his hands,
if in the meantime he loses his soul and inevitably damns himself through sins?
In all the kingdoms he cannot find anything to give in exchange for it (that is all worthless), and that is true; he himself must be there to pay.
For when the Lord passes judgment, he repays everyone according to what they did and worked here.
Some of those standing here among you (I tell you this for certain) will not taste death or suffer its pain
before they see the holy Son of God in his glory, shining like the sun in his kingdom."
Eight days after this (I mention it here so that you may read for yourself there about the marvellous wonder
that he soon went on to do), he went up a mountain. There you will also read, without doubt, that he told three to go with him;
and there they suddenly saw his glory, and how he also wished to bless them there with things beyond words.
The Father made it sweeter still by greeting his beloved, saying that he was his only one (you know more about this).
Moses the faithful and the renowned Elijah came there to meet him from the holy multitude.
Luke tells you what their business there was, and what his servants spoke steadfastly there with Christ.
Then the disciples were suddenly startled by the radiance, and they were greatly afraid of what happened;
"Go," he then said, "go home now, daughter, in peace and in good, healed in this way by faith.
Truly, your faith made you whole here; it did what was fitting, so that you received the benefit here." You can
read in this account a great many miracles, certainly, as I tell you, all of which he performed:
How the devils went out there at Peter's house, when the Lord resolved to heal his mother-in-law.
Then in the evening all the sick came; he drove away all their sicknesses and their infirmities.
He commanded the winds and the stormy waves; as soon as he spoke of it there, they immediately grew still.
When his disciples called to him while he slept in the boat, terrified with fear, he worked that miracle.
He also healed the blind, who were mourning and who came hurrying to him on the way.
Those who struggled with the devil also came hastening to him, and lepers too; he healed them all at once.
Read for yourself Matthew's part, how a leper was healed; and in Luke's part, how ten were healed.
Old bedridden people are also told of there, sick men; he healed them all, as was fitting.
Above all he wiped out their sin, which was a wonder; in his goodness he forgave them their misdeeds.
Add to these a great many blind people, a multitude of lame people, and a gathering of crippled people,
whom I cannot list in full, even if I spent the day on it, or the whole year, and my life beyond that.
This happened in the settlements [?] and out in the countryside, wherever they cried out and hurried to meet him:
the Lord healed them all at once; I tell you that in all truth. Whoever approached him went away happier.
Whoever cared to seek help from him (know it in all truth) lacked nothing there;
for he himself is joy and the fountain of all good; truly, all good flowed from him there
in abundance to all people, to whoever spoke of it there, to whoever ran there for this purpose and called out to him there.
In this manner he sent out twelve disciples (yet not for worldly glory), to work miracles as well;
so that they would put devils to flight in wretched sicknesses and always help the people in all their needs.
He commanded them to take heed and to take nothing with them at that time as provision for the road,
neither purse nor bag, and to set out from there in this way; nor to carry any penny with them on that mission;
that they should undertake it in this way and go with staffs, with rods in their hands, in great haste;
and that they should not care to seek two tunics for themselves, nor many kinds of shoes in that haste.
And each of them then set about it; one after another they went and took themselves out of that place when they heard this;
for each of them there now understood that the man ought to be good who would count himself among the good and would torment the sinful woman in this way.
In truth they were not that. So they shied away there, and at once, on the same path, they withdrew from the matter.
The Lord was left there, and she was alone; her heart was sore within her, and she still stood there in the middle.
"Woman," he said, "now tell me: where are those who were against you, who gathered here for this purpose and accused you so hatefully just now?
Does anyone here condemn you now?" She answered as was fitting: "No one, Lord," she said. "That is all through your power!"
"Nor do I condemn you," he said. "Now go forth, and see that you always take care that you sin no more." — Mercy
on me too, Lord! I am your sinful servant, sinful in thoughts and in hateful deeds!
What would my punishment be, were it not for your mercy, because of my evil deeds and my manifold wickedness?
Help me, Lord, in my need, as you did here just now for this poor woman, so that the lust of adultery may not cling to me;
so that I do not go astray, and always place my hope in you, and so that I may always be, my Lord, your constant servant! — Again
the Lord told them that he is the chosen light, and wholly without blame in his deeds.
He showed them much good there, but none of it went into their minds; nothing of the Lord's teaching went into their ears.
XVIII. WHICH OF YOU CONVICTS ME OF SIN?
Among many words and very weighty matters, the Lord, by his own power, then spoke to them thus:
"Who is there here among you," he said, "who can accuse me of this? Who among you will charge me with sin?
If I tell you the truth here, why do you not believe me at once? Why do your minds not open when I tell you what is good?
Know this: whoever is from God hears his word, and always turns his own heart to it very readily.
In truth you are not from him. That is why you do not hear it at once, and why his manifold goodness does not come into your minds."
They began to answer with very harsh words, and to argue with him there with base words.
"What," they said, "do we say wrongly if the devil is in you? We will tell you something more as well: you are an utter foreigner!"
"Know," he said, "that I certainly do not have the devil. I am wholly safe from that; he has no part with me.
Rather, I honour my Father above all, as I ought. I do not hide this from you: but you dishonour me!
I do not seek dominion here now, nor my own glory. My Father looks to that, and he himself judges!
Know this for certain: those who keep my word, who willingly fulfil what my words tell them — Not …
When he brought it about in this way, and touched us with such things, with his birth, so that it would be to our benefit:
Those deeds did us much good, and afterwards [we] could see, surely enlightened out of the old darkness.
Let everyone now run to the beautiful baptism, to which Christ then directed him and himself sent him there.
Know this in all truth: the water there is also called by this name, because Christ rules it, who was sent here;
No man would ever be healed of his sins if the Father had not sent him and turned him here into the world.
He enlightened us very greatly, and he came here into the world so that his goodness might open our eyes;
So that we might recognize where we should go, on straight paths, to his glorious righteousness;
And that we may behold him with open eyes, face to face, unveiled, so that it may be well with us;
With an open mind, so that it may turn out to our good, may we forever behold him with the eyes of the heart! Amen.
XXII. The Feast of Dedication took place.
Around that time came the dedication of God's house; the people celebrated those same high feasts.
The gospel says there that it was in wintertime, above all this deed that I am now to tell you here.
Then the Lord went inside, into the porch of the house; its name made it famous: that it was Solomon's.
That may truly have been because of its splendor, that people attributed it to him and chose that name for it.
The Jews surrounded him; they did not know what they were doing. They spoke to him treacherously, as they were accustomed:
"How long shall we endure it that you lure us this way toward you, and thus take [?] one by one [?]? Will you forever [?] in this?
If Christ is your name, then let that be made open; tell it to us here, right now, so that we may know it to be true!"
"If I tell it to you," he said, "you still will not believe because of it; your mind does not grasp it when I tell you what is good.
The works that I do in the name of my Father bear witness to me in every way, very fully.
Yet you still do not believe, though it has often been told to you; surely you are not among those whom I choose for myself!
Those whom I count for this and choose apart for myself always have love for me and hear my voice;
I also know them, and they follow me with love; and I truly give them eternal life.
They will never perish; they also escape woe; they are held firmly, without end, in my own hands.
No hatred of men (surely you know this) will take them out of my Father's hand until the end of the world!
What my Father has granted me is the foremost of all good; there is nothing that ever equals the benefits of his gift.
And they fall by force before their enemies, under their hands, by spears and by swords;
They are altogether in flight from that deed, terrified by the works of their fleeing thoughts.
But he died for this need, so that he might gather us, and by the goodness of his death joined us together;
And through his pain we have had a bold heart, ever ready then to stand against our enemies;
So that, glad of that death, we travel homeward into our own estate after this misery.
After they condemned him, as Caiaphas told us, and they put him to death, as he declared there:
Now we are glad in mind because of his one good deed; with his one fall he has redeemed us all!
Now let us dwell boldly in that kingdom of his, joyful in righteousness in his sight.
That same joy his goodness gives us, for he alone achieved this: that he died for us.
Now let us hasten to think of this and work constantly, so that it may always please him, toward the high kingdom of heaven,
And that the Lord may count us all there by name, and name us all there, man by man;
So that his death may not, above all, be in vain in us through our wickedness and our manifold presumption;
But rather let us be bold in this: to rejoice forever with his own, to be glad forever with his own, and not to shun it!
That is made certain for them, that they lack nothing more; so may it also be for all of us, by the will of Christ himself! Amen. Here ends the third book.

XI. Jesus, knowing that his hour had come, etc.
They quickly covered the road for him there, very beautifully; the men hurried eagerly to do it with their garments.
They strewed the road there especially for him, which was a wonder; a strange thing: they spread out their cloaks.
Whoever lacked one at once broke off branches, so that he made the road straight and smooth with them.
They saw to it and broke off branches from the trees there, so that they might gladly strew the road for him.
Many men went there ahead of the king, and a host, also full of eloquent speech, followed behind.
He rode in the middle, as was fitting and as it then fell out on that journey, with honour, as he wished and as a king himself should.
Then they raised a lofty song, very beautiful, fitting for him and very eloquent:
"You rule many people, son of King David; you are also clearly king of the people of this land!
May he have salvation forever, and blessings shared by all, and benefit in glory over all his kingdom!
May he be greatly blessed, for he came in the name of God; Christ the good himself is a king dear to us!
Hail to you also in the highest, with the same blessing; extend your kingdom also into the high kingdom of heaven,
so that you keep us safe here and also rule over the angels, and shine forth there in power over paradise itself!"
Those same good people, all of one mind, sang the delight of this song with a single voice.
The people in front sang it eagerly over and over, and the host behind answered with the same words in turn.
They came with a throng in that same procession, and with that force went straight into the city.
All who were inside were alarmed; it stirred the hearts, I think, of the townspeople themselves.
"Who is this man," they said, "who presses on us here so boldly, crowds us here like this with a host, and pushes us out of the city?"
The people at once gave answer: "This is truly the prophet! The Saviour from Nazareth, who came from there into this land!"
He went into the house of God and drove them all out of it; he forcefully scattered all their wickedness.
By day he taught them and preached in person; by night he always stayed on the Mount of Olives.
It was an unfitting and terrible thing that they begrudged him in their hearts and refused him lodging.
The chief men saw this and were greatly alarmed by it, and they also talked a great deal about these deeds:
"Our cause," they said, "is nothing; it does not prosper any further at all. It can never prosper in the face of this same man.
If this is allowed, this whole world will go after him in a single moment!"
V. Spiritually (Spiritaliter).
I myself will be there for that purpose, and there I will also speak out of you. Be watchful in heart, good, and very steadfast in mind!"
He also told them truly about the last day, and he spoke to them carefully of the time of the Antichrist.
"The affliction the world will suffer then, alas! I will certainly not hide it from you: it will be unlike any other time!
They will then be in woes and grievous hardships, such that no such disaster ever happened before, nor shall one ever happen again.
The Lord will soon shorten it by his grace for the sake of his beloved ones, for the sake of those [?] of God.
The moon and the sun will be joyless in darkness, and the stars will fall to earth from very far away.
Then all that is here on earth will weep over that destruction; all this human race will weep over that same misery!
Then they will see the Son of Man himself coming down here from the clouds with power, to the judgment.
His angels too, in truth: they will blow their horns there, and every one of them will blow very mightily,
so that they may diligently gather all his beloved ones there, and these will come to him there, wherever in the world they may be!
As for what any of you now says about this last time: there is no one who can make it known except my Father alone.
Nor does any man in the world know when it will happen, when God wills that the whole world should fall to ruin.
Yet before it there will certainly be a great calm, as there once was among the people in the days of old Noah.
As the water overtook them there as soon as he had gone into the ark, so suddenly will the Son of Man himself come here.
Therefore always be careful and very watchful, for it is hidden from all of you when the Lord will come!
If the man who is at home in his stronghold knew all the outrage, and how the thief would come,
he would have to keep watch at that time, drive the thief out of there, and not let his house be broken into.
So he keeps watch all night, even though it is beyond his strength, so that he may save what is his and defend it against enemies.
Do as he does, for you do not know the time. Always be watchful, as I have commanded, so that you escape the distress!"
He then told his beloved ones a parable about the ten maidens, one that was apt and fitting for this:
how the five who were unprepared fared, who were not properly watchful, and so failed there;
and how well it went there for those who were always watchful here, who ruled their hearts here and kept them pure.
He also told another parable, so that they would be on guard all the more: how a rich man went into another kingdom;
how, as he had planned beforehand, he divided his treasure among his servants to be worked with carefully.
"He commanded them to look after it and to earn fitting profit with it until he came back.
They said that he did not want the people to pay tribute any longer in honour of the emperor;
and that he had stirred up all the people to strife, to great rebellion: "lest he be let go!
He never left off until he had truly and gravely troubled this whole land with his own teaching;
there is no limit to it and no turning back, the way he leads the land astray, the way he throws it all into confusion and disturbs this world!
He began such things at the far end of this realm, and from there he went through the whole land, until he was seized here just now!"
"Take him yourselves," he said; "why did you bring him to me for this? Judge him there as your law teaches.
If you all find out there how far he seeks what is right, you carry out all of it yourselves; it is known to you, not to me!"
That, they said, was not fitting for them, nor could it be, because their books warned them against killing a man.
By this the people signified what the Lord had said before: that he was to end his life at the hands of heathens.
Yet I tell you truly: they were his killers; they brought him to death with the sharpness of their tongues!
XXI. Pilate's address to Christ in the praetorium.
Then Pilate went back with him into the upper hall and spoke with him at length; he was troubled about these matters.
First he asked about what he feared most: "Tell me now at once," he said, "whether you are their king.
Were you consecrated to it, as the people accuse you? Did you set out with that intention, to seize the kingdom like this?"
Then the Lord said: "Tell me, do you say this of yourself, or did others tell it to you and report it to you about me?"
Pilate wanted to rid him of that idea at once, so that he would not think Pilate had thought it up himself.
"People know of themselves," he said, "that I am not a Jew; your own nation has handed you over to me in this plight.
The people who handed you over to me laid the charge against you; those same people all told me of this boldness of yours.
But if it is true that you are not their king, why is it that they seized you and handed you over to me bound like this?"
"I tell you this," he said: "my kingdom is not from here; it is not, as I explain to you, of the things of this world.
If it were from here, my thanes would strive with their courage, so that my enemy would not overpower me like this
and would not handle me like this in this plight; they would act with valour to rescue me from them.
But I give you the reason: my kingdom is not from here, so that I would defend myself now with an army of my own."
Then Pilate spoke again, because the matter weighed heavily on him; again he asked urgently about his lordship:
"Wherever your kingdom and your glory may be, are you nevertheless truly a king, as I hear?"
Then Christ went out in that procession in a red garment, crowned with thorns and scourged and mocked in this way;
He was forced to wear purple clothing then, and a crown of thorns: that was done to him in mockery.
"Behold," he said, "now the man: he has been condemned to the utmost! You see his disgrace; what more do you want?
He has been harshly reviled, with mocking words as well, and has also been punished very severely for his misdeeds;
He has been scourged," he said, "and set about with thorns as well; now that such things are done to him, let your anger cool!"
When they saw him, they all cried out at once (their hearts burned against him, as enemies' hearts often do),
Then they demanded again and again that he be put to death, and cried out very fiercely: "Crucify him, crucify!"
"Take him yourselves," he said, "and crucify him among you; I cannot find in him that he is so very guilty."
The high priests answered him harshly, out of their old hatred; they could not restrain themselves:
"He must die, as our law shows, and die by his own words at the hands of these men;
For he proclaimed here that he himself is the Son of God, and he truly spread such reports everywhere.
The law teaches that whoever presumptuously claims such a thing for himself is to be hanged on a cross."
Pilate was then greatly afraid at these words; he left them and went with Christ into the praetorium.
"Tell me now at once," he said, "what land you are from, and of what birth, that you have ever come to this."
He stood, kept silent and quietly held his peace; in his patience he gave him no answer.
"Will you not speak to me?" he said. "Do you not know what I am telling you: that your end lies in my own hand;
And that I also have power over everything that concerns you, over life and death today, whichever of the two I command?"
Then the eternal emperor, the heavenly king, gently answered the governor there, truly:
"I tell you, and I do not hide it from you: you would have no power over me if it had not been granted to you from heaven;
Therefore the one who gave me into your hands bears the greater sin, as does the one who brought matters to the point that I am treated like this here."
XXIV. Pilate wished to release Jesus, and how he handed him over to them.
Pilate was then eager to release him: he wanted not to listen to them, and to take him out of that danger.
When they saw this, they raised their voices; the whole crowd of people shouted fiercely against him:
"We accuse you of disloyalty, a grave offense, because you are letting the emperor's enemy go free and unharmed like this.
He has stirred up this whole land; that is why we handed him over to you. He has incited the people to rebellion, and now you are letting him go like this?"
Then a great multitude of the people came out to meet him, and they all followed him to the fall of his own death.
The women of the people of the land then wept loudly, for they too lamented what, alas, they held against him;
They wept loudly then and cried out very bitterly; the wretched grief there touched them in their hearts.
They beat their breasts in their anguish and kept lamenting in their distress over the miserable deeds;
They began to ask why they should torment the one who always meant good for them and healed the whole land!
"Whoever touches him carries good away from him; whoever ventures to come to him goes away from him glad.
He healed lepers as soon as he willed it, all by his powers; what do they blame him for, the Lord!
Blind men seeing and the crippled walking; yes, and dead men too, indeed, came alive at his word;
Yes, it is said in truth that they rose up from the bier, that they began their life again and rose out of the graves!
There is nothing good in the world that he did not do here among us; now shall they destroy him, sinless as he is, so senselessly?
Why do they now crush him like this and put out the good that was in him? If we must now do without him, may God have pity on it!
In him there was great good of many kinds, always plenty of every good thing, for any man who asked for it!"
They wept a long time, [their weeping] reaching up to heaven [?]; the Lord himself looked at them then and spoke to them like this:
"Listen here, women," he said, "do not weep for my life, do not lament my death! I am not to escape it.
Do not lament my suffering; something else will come upon you, more [than this]. Weep for yourselves; you will have great need to.
Weep also, as I tell you, for all your children, because of such distress as the world has never seen before!
For the time is yet to come when every woman will say of another: Happy is she alive who never had children;
Truly blessed is she who is without a child, who never brought one forth from her womb and never nursed one at her breasts!
The times of misery are yet to come upon you, such pitiful conditions of wretchedness;
Such things will yet come home to you that you will waste away to the bone, and such pain will touch soul and heart,
That in your sorrows you will call out to these mountains and ask them (this I tell you) to fall on you;
And you will also ask the hills to cover you from above and shield you in your distress from such times!
Then you will begin to cry out, and to sleep inside the earth, and you will waste away terribly because of such deeds.
Now that they bring things to this, destroying the green tree like this, burning it here like this with the fire of the cross:
What do you think will then become of the useless wood, when they begin to harm the dry tree?"
His beloved friend also stood there alone, pure in virginity; he too happened to be there and saw the misery that had come upon him.
Out of his goodness, then, in this distress, the good son entrusted his mother to him,
so that he would take her to himself and she would not be without comfort; in exchange for her child, he was to care for her in all things.
He provided for his mother while hanging there like that; let us also carry out his command and think of our mother.
33. The sun was darkened, and Jesus gave up the spirit.
The sun was greatly angered at such deeds; she would not let the people of the world see her lordly light.
She quickly withdrew from the wretched deed; in her grief she would not look down on them there.
She would not let them enjoy her beautiful face; for that reason she would not let her bright countenance shine on them.
The brightness I have now told of, in which the world always rejoiced, she denied them, as she had to, for three hours of the day.
That was, in all truth, from the sixth hour to the ninth, which truly should have been the brightest part of the day for them.
She withdrew her bright light from them entirely; she turned it for them into fearful darkness,
for she saw her Lord seized and hanged, the very one who made her, and she was greatly afraid at that.
Then, when the ninth hour came, he cried out very loudly, and his voice addressed his Father's love:
"My Lord, my Lord! Why have you forgotten me, so utterly forsaken me and abandoned me to my enemies?"
They tormented him further and pressed vinegar on him, a bitter drink; they did all this out of malice.
Soon afterwards the Lord cried out again (you can read it there) with a loud voice, which the people there heard:
"Into your hand, Father, I give my soul; I commend to you also, as you know, my own spirit!"
At that very moment he released his soul into his own Father's hand, as he had said just before; so it is told.
One of the soldiers saw this and pierced him to the life; he hurried up with a spear and opened his side.
In this way the meadow, the entrance to the kingdom of heaven, was opened to us; the side opened for us what we had waited for so very long.
Blood and water flowed out of it at once; I tell you truly, we were redeemed by these two.
Then at once the curtain of God's house was torn, the one hung there for the purpose of separating off the cherubim,
the precious altar and indeed the table, and all the lampstands; the curtain fared no better:
it was torn apart then and left nothing covered, because these things were to be made known to us as signs.
Whatever all this signified and always meant for our good, the Lord Christ did it there and then, so that it is open to us.
XXXIV. THE EARTH QUAKED, THE ROCKS WERE SPLIT.
The earth trembled, for the power of God compelled it; and in the same way the stones split apart.
The graves opened, and the dead came out, here into the world: the bodies of the blessed.
I shall tell you a wonder: they went out of the graves, into the city to the people, and showed themselves to them,
so that this news would not stay hidden, and the people themselves would come to know all these deeds.
I tell it here openly: many who were dear to God rose then together with the Lord himself, his beloved servants.
All this was done when the Lord himself chose to rise, and for this we are now glad; he was the firstfruits.
The gospels tell it just as I recount it to you; those same holy books tell it very beautifully.
The centurion himself was greatly frightened by it; after these works he stood there giving thanks to God.
He said that without doubt this man had power over all things, and he declared publicly that he was the Son of God.
The people turned back at once in great sorrow; late in the day they went home from those wretched deeds.
Then they regretted those deeds and beat their breasts, and at once they set off homeward, all full of sorrow.
All those who knew him stood far off, with grieving hearts; yet for them it turned out well in the end.
Those same women who had been with him, and had come to the Passover, then mourned him who was their very life.
XXXV. HOW JOSEPH AND NICODEMUS BURIED JESUS.
Then a noble man came boldly, as was fitting for him; he was angered by these deeds, as a good man should be.
He had not taken part in those deeds or in the plot itself; it had not been his will to carry out such a thing.
He went boldly away from them, in to the governor, and asked that the man be given to him, even though he was now dead,
so that he might take him away, take the body down, and also see to it that he was laid in the grave.
Pilate said he would do just as he asked, and ordered that the body be handed over to him there at once.
Read all the books there are: you will not find, by my faith, that anyone ever did such a thing, or asked for so precious a treasure,
or that anyone in the world ever laid such a treasure on a bier or a litter, I tell you truly.
It was worth more than the angels and the whole kingdom of heaven, the earth and the sea, even though they treated him like this, alas!
Nicodemus the good, who had once come to him by night, came there willingly while he [Joseph] was taking him down.
He truly brought with him a very precious ointment to anoint Christ, as was then the custom there.
It was truly the morning of the Easter feast, and the glory of that day was very great and famous.
On the evening before Sunday the women rose up at once. They did not delay then; they hurried to the tomb.
Surely each of them hurried then because of the late hour. What the holy day had delayed, love made good for them.
They carried their ointment with them on that journey, to anoint Christ, the beloved man.
And as they went they reflected that it could not be that they would roll the weight of the stone away from the tomb.
They thought they would ask men to do it. Their strength was too little against the heaviness of the stone.
They hurried quickly on the way and saw the tomb. To their great surprise, they found the chain [?] unfastened.
Then at that moment there was a great earthquake and a very great terror, so that they were frightened.
The whole earth shook mightily, and quickly it gave up there the treasure that lay in it.
An angel came suddenly from the height of the kingdom of heaven. He rolled the stone away at once, as soon as he touched it.
(Not that he hurried there to clear the way, but so that people would recognize the wondrous deeds,
and also so that people would know that Christ had risen from his resting place. He gave them the empty tomb to see in its bareness.)
His appearance was (what joy!) as beautiful as the sun ever is. All his clothing was the color of white snow.
Then those who guarded the tomb were struck with terror there, all at once [?], and they suddenly became afraid.
In that same distress they became like dead men. Then the angel at once spoke to the women about one beloved person:
"Women, I say to you: do not be afraid at all! Do not let your hearts be troubled; you came here for a good purpose.
How could it ever be that you should be afraid of us? Truly, we are your own neighbors.
I know why you have come here: you are looking for our Savior, whom these people killed and also buried here,
whom they put to death here, tortured on the cross, on whom they took their revenge, and whom they pierced with their spears.
Truly, you have no need. You have nothing of him here. He left nothing undone, just as he himself promised.
He has escaped from hell and has risen up from death. You have no need to mourn him; indeed, this was promised to you.
In the kingdom of death he won the victory mightily. He fights with it no more and no longer rises against it.
I also tell you lovely good news: there he took his spoils, after he had overcome death there, and led them into another land,
into heavenly glory, his own kingdom, mightily and very far, as was fitting for him.
As was fitting for him, he took everything from death. Believe my word: he left nothing of his there.
Before that, he had told them what was still to come: that they would seize him and hang him on the cross.
XVI. On the Ascension of the Lord.
When the Lord wished to set out on a journey to visit his own kingdom, after the victory, as was fitting, that he had won over Satan,
from whom he rescued us, and whom he laid low in hell, and also won us by force into his own homeland,
he then gave his disciples a command with these words, that they should understand it well and come to meet him.
He commanded them to hurry, at those same fair times, to the place he had in mind and had himself pointed out to them.
They hurried there without fail, as he himself had commanded them. They made the journey just as they were used to, and worshipped the Lord himself.
Then he came closer to them and welcomed them sweetly, though first he rebuked them harshly with his own words
for having hearts so hard in that adversity [?] that they did not at once believe those who had seen him risen.
Since he was about to leave them, he told them a great deal, so that it would stay firm in the breast of their hearts.
There he also told them many things in a wealth of words, and the Lord also spoke thus:
"In heaven and on earth I rule over all of it. All the ends of the world are given into my hand.
Now I shall send you out and turn you to my service. Tell the peoples of the world all that I command you.
Go out preaching as far as this world extends, and proclaim all these things over the whole circle of the world.
Tell them also very boldly that I myself came here into the world, so that my presence might soften their hardness.
Make my own teaching widely known among them. Baptize them and preach, so that they believe in God.
Go to the poor and the rich alike, to whatever has life on earth, whether man or woman.
If they hasten to it and take hold of the faith, let them all be baptized; then that is their salvation.
But whoever does not hasten to it and does not consecrate himself through baptism, and therefore truly does not believe, is already condemned.
You have power to work signs throughout the lands of the world, the ones you saw me do while you were with me.
Heal lepers as soon as you resolve to; drive sicknesses away as soon as you touch them.
Raise the dead wherever you pray to me for it. Old bedridden people are to be counted among these too.
This power is shared among you, so that there is truly no sickness in the world that you will not heal at once.
The devil cannot stand against it wherever you name my name. Wherever you begin this, you are wrestling against him.
So you have no need to fear: I am always with you. You will not lack me any more. Do not fear the pain at all!"
Lead thither, Lord, by your own might, to that beautiful life, your faithful servants,
so that we may enjoy that delight under your protection, in our hearts, forever, for our good!
Those whom we call martyrs have made it known that there, in that vision, there is very much beauty;
and their hearts revealed that there is very much good there, when they strove for it here and died for that same beauty;
They paid no heed to the harm of weapons, nor to scourging by men, nor to burning by fire;
That other life was more in their minds than the manifold pain, more than the torment of the body at that time.
In their distress their bodies became dead, while their souls became very rich in the high kingdom of heaven.
Let us too take into our hearts that very manifold good, and let us set our thoughts on it as well, to obtain the kingdom of heaven;
let us constantly beg for it with thoughtful care and with great love, here among the men of the world!
Let us flee the evils that come over us here; let us hasten, comforted and set free, to the kingdom of heaven!
Here many infirmities truly cling to us; thirst and hunger, these do not harm us there.
Shield us, good Lord, from these troubles, body and soul, for your own glory;
through your goodness grant us this kindness, that by your grace we may escape this toil!
Here many things grieve us; there we do not worry about that. Here we have many anxieties; there we have delights.
This is the dominion of death; there is life pure and simple, for the kingdom of heaven is the kingdom of the living.
No one there rejoices in heart except the simple and good, who here always earnestly did the command of the gospel;
those who here always gladly fulfilled what the books told them, the law, diligently; they will enjoy it greatly there.
Here there is always woe and pain at all times, and very heavy hours; this you know for certain;
immeasurable pain, which we never overcome unless it comes to us, weary as we are, from the Lord's grace.
Shield us, good Lord, from these troubles, body and soul, for your own glory;
through your goodness grant us this kindness, that by your grace we may escape this toil!
Let us always hasten away from here; alas, we went forth from there, out of the hands of paradise into grievous exile;
from the sweetness of the kingdom of heaven into miserable punishment, into this earthly valley; we lost all that other life completely;
into this valley of tears, which we now feel grievously, into the burden of this weeping, which has never been lacking to us since.
